extraction.name: Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD)
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of 100,000+ crowdworker-posed questions on Wikipedia articles, where each answer is a text span from the corresponding passage.
extraction.creator: Pranav Rajpurkar and Jian Zhang and Konstantin Lopyrev and Percy Liang
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected in three stages: curating Wikipedia passages, crowdsourcing question-answer pairs on those passages, and obtaining additional answers for development and test questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In additional answer collection, some questions were marked unanswerable by at least one crowdworker.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source was English Wikipedia articles and their extracted paragraphs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Paragraphs were extracted from sampled Wikipedia articles, with images, figures, and tables removed, and paragraphs shorter than 500 characters discarded; articles were then randomly partitioned into train, development, and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers created up to 5 questions per paragraph, entered questions in a text field, and highlighted answer spans in the paragraph; additional annotators later selected the shortest answer span for development and test questions or marked questions as unanswerable.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Daemo platform with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was estimated using multiple answers per question, and disagreement was attributed mostly to inclusion or exclusion of non-essential phrases rather than fundamental disagreements.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 answers per question in the development and test sets
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotator location in the United States or Canada
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset contains ambiguous examples where the authors did not agree with the crowdworkers' answer or the question did not have a unique answer.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Answers are constrained to spans in the passage, making the questions more constrained than more interpretative questions in advanced standardized tests.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and test for machine reading comprehension and question answering research.

name.evidence: To address the need for a large and high-quality reading comprehension dataset, we present the Stanford Question Answering Dataset v1.0 (SQuAD), freely available at https://stanford-qa.com

description.evidence: We present the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), a new reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text from the corresponding reading passage.

url.evidence: The dataset is freely available athttps://stanford-qa.com .

creator.evidence: Pranav Rajpurkar and Jian Zhang and Konstantin Lopyrev and Percy Liang

inLanguage.evidence: we used Project Nayuki’s Wikipedia’s intemal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We collect our dataset in three stages: curating passages, crowdsourcing question-answers on those passages, and obtaining additional answers.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Passage curation. To retrieve high-quality articles, we used Project Nayuki’s Wikipedia’s intemal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia, from which we sampled 536 articles uniformly at random. Question-answer collection. Next, we employed crowdworkers to create questions.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: Over the development and test sets, 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one of the additional crowdworkers.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: we used Project Nayuki’s Wikipedia’s intemal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia, from which we sampled 536 articles uniformly at random. From each of these articles, we extracted individual paragraphs

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: From each of these articles, we extracted individual paragraphs, stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. The result was 23,215 paragraphs for the 536 articles covering a wide range of topics, from musical celebrities to abstract concepts. We partitioned the articles randomly into a training set (80%), a development set (10%), and a test set (10%).

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: On each paragraph, crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions on the content of that paragraph. The questions had to be entered in a text field, and the answers had to be highlighted in the paragraph. To get an indication of human performance on SQuAD and to make our evaluation more robust, we obtained at least 2 additional answers for each question in the development and test sets. In the secondary answer generation task, each crowdworker was shown only the questions along with the paragraphs of an article, and asked to select the shortest span in the paragraph that answered the question. If a question was not answerable by a span in the paragraph, workers were asked to submit the question without marking an answer.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: We used the Daemo platform (Gaikwad et al., 2015), with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Recall that each of the questions in these sets has at least three answers. To evaluate human performance, we treat the second answer to each question as the human prediction, and keep the other answers as ground truth answers. Mismatch occurs mostly due to inclusion/exclusion of non-essential phrases (e.g., monsoon trough versusmovement of the monsoon trough ) rather than fundamental disagreements about the answer.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: Recall that each of the questions in these sets has at least three answers.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: The non-numerical answers are categorized using constituency parses and POS tags generated by Stanford CoreNLP.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Ambiguous We don’t agree with the crowdworkers’ answer, or the question does not have a unique answer.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: While questions with span-based answers are more constrained than the more interpretative questions found in more advanced standardized tests, we still find a rich diversity of questions and answer types in SQuAD.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We partitioned the articles randomly into a training set (80%), a development set (10%), and a test set (10%).
